0-eNNTf-TrQ.title: Jetashree Ravi: Stop Renting Intelligence: The Train-to-Deploy Loop for Specialized AI
0-eNNTf-TrQ.label: The AI Conference
0-eNNTf-TrQ.description:
The next wave of AI products will not rely only on prompting generic frontier models. Winning teams will own specialized models shaped by their product data, user feedback, and domain workflows. In this 25-minute session, we’ll cover the practical loop behind model ownership: choose a base model, prepare data, fine-tune with SFT/DPO/RL, evaluate outputs, deploy the tuned model, collect feedback, and repeat. We’ll also explain why training and inference should be treated as one system, not separate steps. Attendees will leave with a simple framework for when to tune, when RL matters, and how continuous improvement turns fine-tuning from a one-off project into a product advantage.

0McYRNmVFFA.title: Dave Sergeant: Why the AI You Love Can't Touch Your Data (Yet)
0McYRNmVFFA.label: The AI Conference
0McYRNmVFFA.description:
You've felt it. You sit down with a frontier AI and watch it do something genuinely brilliant. So why isn't that capability showing up in your work? Two reasons: you can't hand company and customer data to a chat window, and your business isn't a chat. It's thousands of repeatable, auditable interactions a day, and nothing about raw model access makes those reliable, private, or provable. That gap is why an estimated 95% of enterprise AI pilots never reach production. At SS&C, we hit this wall at scale, processing billions of tokens a month across a regulated, global business, and had to build the layer that closes it: guardrails, monitoring, and auditing between the model and the work. In ten minutes, we'll show you what that layer looks like, why every organization needs one, and what changes when it exists.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

Why Knowledge Graphs are Necessary for Enterprise AI

Knowledge graphs add explicit knowledge to GenAI in a format that is easily understood by humans and enhances enterprise machine decisions. They are rapidly emerging as a useful & often necessary component of GenAI, complementing what is otherwise a world of statistical reasoning rooted in inferred concepts. Knowledge graphs make GenAI more dependable, transparent, and secure across a wide variety of use cases, opening the door further for GenAI adoption.

This talk presents a framework for how to think about knowledge graphs for any use case. You will hear up-to-date learnings from this evolving field, including design patterns & examples derived from working with many of the world’s largest organizations. You will come away with an understanding of how knowledge graphs can play the role of left brain to the right brain that is the universe of LLM + vectors– in an enterprise landscape where many use cases call for the use of both hemispheres.

0hpdbtS4VtA.title: Hardik Nahata & Deepika Khera: Building Agentic AI at PayPal: Platform, Governance, and Agent Design
0hpdbtS4VtA.label: The AI Conference
0hpdbtS4VtA.description:
An agent that can act on production systems is a new actor in the enterprise. It has credentials, and it can accomplish complex tasks across systems autonomously. That changes what the platform underneath has to provide: identity and authorization for non-human actors, transaction-grade reliability, and observability that treats every agent action as a first-class audited event. At PayPal we run a fleet of specialized agents on shared infrastructure — agents that write code, deploy models, and monitor agents. They sit on a common substrate: a certified agent/mcp registry, agent-to-agent delegation, unified model routing under latency and cost pressure, enterprise memory that persists across sessions, and a governed skills layer so capabilities are reused rather than rebuilt. We're now extending that substrate across cloud project boundaries, so agents owned by different teams and deployed in different environments can find and delegate to each other. Once agents cross those boundaries, identity and audit become essential. In regulated financial infrastructure, governance, security, and Responsible AI aren't a layer bolted on, they're the substrate the swarm of agents runs on. This talk walks through that architecture, then gets into the parts that were hard to learn: graph-based orchestration with typed state contracts, how we scaled the agent orchestrator, normalizing two agent protocols into one response contract, human-in-the-loop at the right moments, and agent memory that survives across sessions. You'll leave with patterns you can apply to your own systems and a clearer view of the platform capabilities these systems rely on.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

4481n9SKrGg.label: The AI Conference
4481n9SKrGg.description:
Scalable End-To-End ML Platforms From Auto ML To Self-Serve

ML platforms help enable intelligent data-driven applications and maintain them with limited engineering effort. Upon sufficiently broad adoption, such platforms reach economies of scale that bring greater component reuse while improving efficiency of system development and maintenance. For an end-to-end ML platform with broad adoption, scaling relies on pervasive ML automation and system integration to reach the quality we term self-serve; a quality we define with ten requirements and six optional capabilities. 

With this in mind, we identify long-term goals for platform development, discuss related tradeoffs and future work. Our reasoning is illustrated on two commercially-deployed end-to-end ML platforms that host hundreds of real-time use cases at Meta — one general-purpose and one specialized.

About Mia Garrard
I am currently a Research Engineer on the Adaptive Experimentation team, and previously led the Personalized Experimentation team at Meta. My current work focuses on lowering the barrier of entry to ML and improving outcomes via AutoML practices. I am interested in causal inference, interpretable/explainable machine learning, and Bayesian Optimization.

Prior to Meta, I worked in the intersection of machine learning and healthcare, and am passionate about applications of AI for science. Specifically, my group researched the development of a novel imaging modality to improve intra-operative decision making in a neurosurgical setting via computer vision methods.

5RuO46cWZek.title: Hai Guan: Right Query, Wrong Answer: Why AI Analytics Is So Hard, and How to Fix It
5RuO46cWZek.label: The AI Conference
5RuO46cWZek.description:
Every product team has an analysis backlog. Questions pile up, same metrics get re-sliced weekly, and when answers finally arrive, validation is manual and inconsistent. At many companies, the ratio is 80% execution mechanics to 20% actual thinking. We wanted the inverse. So we built AI Analyst - an open-source, multi-agent system powered by Claude Code that automates the full analytical workflow: from a business question to a validated, stakeholder-ready slide deck in roughly 30 minutes instead of days and weeks. What We built: The system orchestrates 18 specialized agents across a 4-phase pipeline - Frame, Analyze, Story, Deck - using DAG-based parallel execution. A Question Framing agent turns vague asks into testable hypotheses. Eight analysis agents run concurrently (descriptive, cohort, root cause, trend, validation, opportunity sizing). A Story Architect designs narrative beats before any chart is created - solving the "chart looking for a story" problem. A Chart Maker generates Storytelling-with-Data-styled visualizations with collision detection. Every output passes through 4-layer validation: structural, logical, business rules, and Simpson's Paradox checks, graded A through F. The system includes a knowledge layer that compounds over time: query archaeology captures proven SQL patterns, a corrections log ensures mistakes are never repeated, and organization-specific context (metrics definitions, business rules, team glossary) accumulates with use. It connects to any data source - CSV, DuckDB, Postgres, BigQuery, Snowflake. What I learned: The hardest part wasn't building the agents - it was getting an organization to trust and adopt AI-assisted analytics. Five real blockers emerged: security and legal approvals, data classification concerns, warehouse access, API cost ownership, and analyst skepticism. I'll share specific tactics for each, including the one that worked best: "show the output, not the pipeline." The critical design principle: AI can execute analysis fast, but it cannot tell you what question to ask or whether the answer makes business sense. We designed the system around human validation, not human replacement. The learning flywheel - run, review, spot errors, correct, store, improve - is what makes the system get meaningfully better over time. This talk is for data leaders, product managers, and engineers who want to democratize analytics without sacrificing rigor.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

When Machines Imagine: Ethical Futures Beyond Human Design

As generative AI systems increasingly produce visions of the future—often without clear authorship or accountability—they raise urgent ethical questions that go beyond traditional frameworks. What does it mean when machines “imagine” on our behalf? What ethical obligations emerge when AI-generated images shape foresight, policy, and public imagination?

In this talk, Alina Solotarov draws from Futures Studies, Information Ethics, and real-world case studies of AI-generated images of the future (AIGIFs) to argue for a radical rethinking of ethical frameworks. Moving beyond compliance and control narratives, she introduces the concept of ethical co-imagination—an approach that integrates transparency, representational justice, and the epistemic integrity of visual foresight.

Drawing on her research at Fraunhofer ISI and her award-winning Master's thesis at Freie Universität Berlin, Alina offers a compelling synthesis of theory and practice. She examines how current frameworks—whether utilitarian, deontological, or regulatory—fail to account for the ontological and semantic ambiguities of machine-generated futures.

This session will equip thought leaders, technologists, and policymakers with fresh tools to evaluate and govern generative AI—not only in terms of harm reduction, but also in terms of who gets to imagine, what is left out, and how we build futures worth living in.

5dRByrcRXec.title: Abbas Raza: Beyond the Demo: Shipping Computer-Use Agents in Production
5dRByrcRXec.label: The AI Conference
5dRByrcRXec.description:
Computer-use agents, AI systems that interact directly with browsers and graphical user interfaces, have rapidly moved from impressive demos to early production deployments. However, operating these agents reliably in real environments introduces a class of challenges that are often underestimated or ignored in early implementations. This talk presents a practical, experience-driven examination of computer-use agents deployed in live business workflows. It traces the evolution from low-level browser control approaches (e.g., DOM- and vision-based interaction) to higher-level abstractions and orchestration layers, highlighting the architectural tradeoffs that emerged only under real-world load, UI drift, and partial system failures. Key topics include: Common failure modes in computer-use agents, including UI volatility, non-deterministic model behavior, timing and synchronization issues, and brittle task decomposition Reliability strategies such as constrained action spaces, verification loops, retries and recovery, fallback paths, and human-in-the-loop controls Observability gaps unique to UI-driven agents and practical techniques for debugging, monitoring, and post-incident analysis Latency, cost, and throughput tradeoffs when scaling computer-use agents beyond isolated tasks Security, compliance, and blast-radius considerations when agents operate on live systems The talk also challenges the assumption that increased autonomy always leads to better outcomes, and proposes a more pragmatic model for deploying computer-use agents as constrained, inspectable systems rather than fully autonomous actors. Attendees will leave with a concrete mental model for evaluating when computer-use agents are appropriate, architectural patterns that improve reliability, and a set of anti-patterns to avoid when moving from demo to production.

David Talby, CEO, Pacific AI

Securing Clinical Trust: Challenges in Evaluating and Monitoring Medical AI

As clinical AI systems become integral to patient care and healthcare operations, organizations’ AI Governance duty to prove that their systems are safe, effective, and legal require robust evaluation and continuous monitoring. This session covers:
Key challenges in effective evaluation of medical AI solutions include data contamination, fragile metrics, benchmarks that lack resemblance to real-world use cases, and the need for localize validation.
Legal requirements including national and state laws, regulations, industry standards, and contractual obligations that require bias, safety, and quality evaluation.
Medical red teaming gaps that must be addressed to uncover ethical, safety, and security vulnerabilities unique to healthcare applications.
Clinical cognitive biases such as anchoring, framing, and sycophancy that impact LLMs as well as humans and can skew AI‑driven recommendations.
MLOps requirements for continuous testing and monitoring, to ensure models remain safe, compliant, and clinically reliable as regulations and data drift evolve.
We’ll explore emerging open-source libraries like MedHELM and LangTest, new research datasets like MedSafetyBench and MedAgentBench, and evolving standards from CHAI and NIST aiming to help address these challenges. Whether you’re building EHR‑powered chatbots or diagnostic decision‑support tools, this session will equip you with the knowledge and tools available today to deliver effective AI Governance for medical applications.

6bSprQfLFUc.title: Elliot Marx: Two Halves of Inference to Build, Eval & Run Agents
6bSprQfLFUc.label: The AI Conference
6bSprQfLFUc.description:
The AI stack is changing, but whether you’re building an agent or fine-tuning an LLM, the same problem remains: you need the right context to build, evaluate, and deploy reliable AI systems. Many failures that look like model or prompt problems are actually context problems, with agents making confident decisions that are inaccurate or based on stale data. Evals have the same context problem. If you evaluate an agent or fine-tuned LLM against non-realistic or incomplete context, you can’t know how it will perform on the tasks and data it will encounter in production. In this hands-on presentation, Chalk Co-Founder Elliot Marx will show how a unified context layer solves both. A context layer is the missing decision infrastructure to give live, governed data to agents and models at inference time - querying your data where it already lives, so every AI decision gets the real-time context it needs. The same system powers testing and evals, so you can prove that your agent is production-ready. With a context layer, you turn data that helps AI understand the world it’s acting on into agent context at the moment of inference - and run the full AI decision system. He’ll demonstrate the full workflow across use cases, from fine-tuning an open-weight LLM and serving it in your own cloud to testing an agent in a simulated time-bound environment with knowledge-cutoff data and tool access, evaluating against real-world tasks, and deploying in a sandbox. Finally, Elliot will share practical lessons from building context and infrastructure for ML and agentic systems used by companies like Whatnot, Turo, and Mission Lane, and a framework for making context and evals a core part of how you build AI.

7FUyuc-AM5Q.title: Stephen Chin | Keynote: GraphRAG: The Definitive Guide - Patterns, Trade-offs & Production Systems
7FUyuc-AM5Q.label: The AI Conference
7FUyuc-AM5Q.description:
Download Stephen Chin’s book here: https://neo4j.com/books/oreilly-graphrag-definitive-guide/ GraphRAG has quickly become a catch-all term for everything from graph-enhanced retrieval to Text2Cypher, agent memory, and community-based summarization. That is exciting, but it also creates confusion. When people say “use GraphRAG,” what do they actually mean, and which pattern fits which problem? This talk gives AI engineers a practical map of the GraphRAG landscape. We start with the limits of vector-only RAG, especially when data is connected, multi-hop, dynamic, or needs to be explainable. From there, we break GraphRAG into a set of core building blocks: constructing knowledge graphs from structured and unstructured data, choosing among lexical, domain, and meta graphs, and applying retrieval patterns such as guided traversal, graph-filtered search, Cypher templates, Text2Cypher, graph embeddings, query-focused summarization, and agentic retrieval. The goal is not to present GraphRAG as one recipe, but as a toolbox with clear trade-offs. We will show when a lightweight pattern is enough, when a richer graph model pays off, and how to think about evaluation, governance, and production readiness from the start. Attendees will leave with a working mental model of GraphRAG, a taxonomy of the most useful patterns, and a decision framework for designing graph-powered GenAI systems that are accurate, explainable, and useful beyond the demo.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

7ajiXYpnOLI.title: Nandini V.: No Agentic Sovereignty, No Agentic Security
7ajiXYpnOLI.label: The AI Conference
7ajiXYpnOLI.description:
For high-security organizations like government, finance, defense, and regulated industries, failing to secure agents isn’t just inconvenient. It’s catastrophic: stalled payments, delayed medical treatments, and dead power grids. More than 70% of regulated-industry leaders name security and privacy as their top barrier to adoption. Agents break the assumptions these industries were built on. Unlike deterministic software, they take actions on their own, reach into live systems, and act with privilege no one formally provisioned. The autonomy is the value. Where it acts, and on whose authority, is the exposure. The instinct is to bolt on data residency and call it solved. It isn't. Data sitting in a database is one thing; data an agent picks up, reasons over, and acts on is another—and that motion is where sovereignty actually breaks. In this session, we’ll detail why regulated industries need truly sovereign solutions to support agents in the environments where they run. We'll examine why data residency alone isn't enough, and unpack the risks across every sovereignty control point an agent touches—data, infrastructure, decision, and ecosystem Attendees will leave understanding the high-risk actions agents can take on their behalf, why probabilistic guardrails satisfy none of these dimensions, and what high-assurance controls — spanning identity, infrastructure, and decision authority—regulated industries actually need before they let agents act. Organizations that treat this as a continuous, auditable posture will be the ones who move fast in AI adoption and still pass the audit.

8XcRxDCzN7c.description:
Taming The Wild West Of LLMs

Large language models (LLMs) have changed the AI landscape in recent months. The pace of innovation in AI has been unprecedented and unlike any other field of science. This fast-paced progress has been possible mainly due to open science and open-access. However, research on benchmarking and evaluation tools has yet to be able to keep up with the growth of the capabilities of these powerful models. 

Brain icon for The AI Conference 2023, a groundbreaking two-day event on AGI, LLMs, Infrastructure, Alignment, AI Startups, and Neural Architectures.

I will discuss the LLM landscape, where open and closed-access models coexist, and what are the pros and cons of each. Next, I will focus on current tooling for evaluating LLMs’ capabilities and vulnerabilities. Finally, I will discuss open challenges and exciting research problems in taming the wild west of LLMs.

About Nazneen Rajani
I am Research Lead at Hugging Face 🤗. Currently, I am part of the team working on building an open-source alternative to ChatGPT called H4. While building such a powerful LLM, I am thinking deeply about evaluation, specifically about the following problems -- 1. Designing and implementing methods for evaluating emerging capabilities, 2. What is the pareto front for the different choices of safety vs. usefulness?, and 3. Quantitative measures for tradeoffs between these choices.

My interests and expertise lie at the intersection of Model Evaluation, Robustness, and Interpretability. My long term research agenda includes 1. Dataset curation for understanding training and evaluation data, 2. Human-in-the-loop training and evaluation for model robustness, 3. Repurposing LLMs and PLMs to make them more usable in the real world. Checkout my HF spaces to see what I am building

Before joing Hugging Face, I was a Senior Research Scientist at Salesforce Research where I worked with Richard Socher and Caiming Xiong on commonsense reasoning and interpretability in NLP. I led a small team focused on building robust natural language generation models. Prior to working at Salesforce, I completed my Ph.D. thesis in the Department of Computer Science at the Machine Learning Research Group of the University of Texas, Austin. I worked with my advisor Prof. Ray Mooney on problems in NLP, Vision and at the intersection of NLP and Vision. I have also worked on problems in Explainable AI (XAI) wherein I proposed a scalable approach to generate visual explanations for ensemble methods using the localization maps of the component systems. Evaluating explanations is also a challenging problem and I proposed two novel evaluation metrics that does not require human generated GT.

I completed my MS in CS with thesis advised by Jason Baldridge on new topic detection using topical alignment from tweets based on their author and recipient.

8ofB2rbIY_k.title: Satyanandam Kotha, Uber: Distributed Real-Time Fraud Detection
8ofB2rbIY_k.label: The AI Conference
8ofB2rbIY_k.description:
Satyanandam Kotha, Staff Software Engineer, Uber 

Distributed Real-Time Fraud Detection: A Scalable Architecture for Combating Fake Reviews in E-Commerce

This presentation introduces a cutting-edge distributed system for real-time fake review detection that addresses critical marketplace integrity challenges while delivering exceptional performance metrics. Our architecture leverages streaming data pipelines built on Apache Flink, Kafka, and Spark Streaming to process reviews as they arrive, enabling immediate identification of fraudulent activity with average detection latencies under 100 milliseconds—a substantial improvement over traditional batch-processing approaches.
The system employs a sophisticated hybrid detection model that combines natural language processing, graph neural networks, and behavioral analytics to identify complex fraud patterns. Our multi-model integration approach demonstrates a 0.94 precision score, significantly outperforming single-architecture alternatives that typically achieve 0.78-0.86 precision. The temporal pattern analysis component can detect coordinated campaigns involving as few as 8 accounts, with marked improvement in early detection rates compared to conventional methods.
For sophisticated collusion networks, our graph-based detection methodology achieves high detection rates for campaigns involving just 12 accounts—far exceeding non-graph approaches for similar operations. The system architecture scales near-linearly to 32 worker nodes with strong efficiency metrics, essential for processing massive review graphs containing 500 million to 3 billion edges.
Privacy and security remain paramount through our federated learning implementation, which achieves detection accuracy comparable to fully centralized approaches while dramatically reducing cross-organizational data exposure. Our differential privacy guarantees maintain F1 scores above 0.92 with privacy parameter ε = 4.6.
Production deployment across multiple e-commerce environments has demonstrated the system's effectiveness, substantially reducing fraudulent review prevalence while maintaining high availability. Resource utilization increases sub-linearly with traffic volume, and the system sustains low latency even at 5x normal traffic—critical for maintaining performance during promotional events when both legitimate and fraudulent review volumes typically spike.
This presentation will provide attendees with architectural insights and implementation strategies for building high-performance fraud detection systems that protect marketplace integrity and consumer trust.

Improving Retrieval Quality For Text Search

To capture the meaning and context of human language, semantic search through vectors can significantly improve the relevance of search results, leading to a better understanding of user queries. AXmHf11Qsmw.title: Dr. Stella Umunna: Kill, Suspend, or Scale? Hands-On AI Governance with the CHOIR-G Framework
AXmHf11Qsmw.label: The AI Conference
AXmHf11Qsmw.description:
The Problem: Standard technical metrics like Accuracy and Recall do not measure real-world risk, especially in high-stakes environments. This workshop moves beyond theoretical AI ethics to provide a hard, quantitative framework for deployment decisions. Participants will learn the CHOIR-G Framework, a risk-weighted scoring model, and apply it in real-time to a notorious healthcare case study, calculating risk to make a definitive "Kill, Suspend, or Scale" deployment decision. As AI systems move from sandbox to production, engineering and leadership teams face a critical "AI Risk Gap." A model may boast high internal performance metrics, but if it fails in a live, dynamic environment, who is harmed? Who owns the risk outcomes? Are core error controls in place at reporting? This 90-minute workshop equips AI builders and strategists with the CHOIR-G Framework: a vendor-neutral, highly actionable governance methodology that bridges technical performance with social trust and enterprise accountability. CHOIR evaluates five core dimensions: Context, Human Impact, Organizational Accountability, Indicators, and Review & Oversight. Instead of passively listening to a lecture, attendees will be put to work. After a brief breakdown of the CHOIR-G mathematics : S = wC * C + wH * H + wO * O + wI * I + wR * R where: S = overall composite score wC = weight assigned to the C dimension wH = weight assigned to the H dimension wO = weight assigned to the O dimension wI = weight assigned to the I dimension wR = weight assigned to the R dimension C = score for the C dimension H = score for the H dimension O = score for the O dimension I = score for the I dimension R = score for the R dimension The room will break into groups to act as a board for governing enterprise AI. The Hands-On Case Study: Groups will be tasked with conducting a governance review of the Epic Systems Sepsis Early Warning System. In internal testing, the model boasted a high AUC-ROC, but in production, University of Michigan researchers (published in JAMA Internal Medicine) found it missed 67% of actual sepsis cases because the model "cheated" by picking up on when doctors were already ordering antibiotics. Given the life-or-death stakes, teams must debate the weights of each CHOIR dimension for this specific deployment, score the system's failure, and determine the necessary governance outcome, ultimately working through the process to establish the strict "Human-in-the-Loop" protocols required to secure such a system. What Attendees Will Walk Away Knowing: • The CHOIR-G Scoring Mechanics: How to implement a 1–15 risk-weighted scoring system for any AI model. • The "Critical 1" Automatic Intervention: How to establish non-negotiable guardrails in their deployment pipelines to prevent catastrophic edge-case failures. • Cross-Functional Translation: How to translate abstract ethical and risk concerns into concrete, quantifiable metrics that engineering, legal, and executive teams can agree on.

BqaOen-jJhI.title: Gradient-Free Structured Pruning With Unlabeled Data, Azade Nova, Research Scientist,Google DeepMind
BqaOen-jJhI.label: The AI Conference
BqaOen-jJhI.description:
Gradient-Free Structured Pruning With Unlabeled Data

Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved great success in solving difficult tasks across many domains, but such success comes with a high computation cost, and inference latency. As developers and third parties customize these models, the need to provide efficient inference has increased. Many efforts have attempted to reduce inference cost through model compression techniques such as pruning and distillation. However, these techniques either require labeled data, or are time-consuming as they require the compressed model to be retrained to regain accuracy. 

Brain icon for The AI Conference 2023, a groundbreaking two-day event on AGI, LLMs, Infrastructure, Alignment, AI Startups, and Neural Architectures.

In this paper, we propose a gradient-free structured pruning framework that uses only unlabeled data. An evaluation on the GLUE and SQuAD benchmarks using BERTBASE and DistilBERT illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach. By only using the weights of the pre-trained model and unlabeled data, in a matter of a few minutes on a single GPU, up to 40% of the original FLOP count can be reduced with less than a 4% accuracy loss across all tasks considered.

About Azade Nova
I am a Senior Research Scientist at Google DeepMind. My research interests lie in the broad area of machine learning, and combinatorial optimization. Currently, my focus is on improving different capabilities of the Large Language models (LLMs). Specifically I am leading the efforts on efficient inference, reasoning, and planning of the LLMs. I have published more than 40 peer-reviewed papers at scientific venues such as Nature, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, VLDB, and SIGMOD. Before joining Google, I was a postdoctoral researcher at Microsoft Research in Data Management, Exploration and Mining DMX group.

My research interests are in the broad areas of social network analysis, graph mining, machine learning, data mining, and database. I completed my PhD in Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Texas, Arlington under the supervision of Dr. Gautam Das in Database Exploration Lab (DBXLAB). My PhD research focused on data exploration and analysis over online community networks such as GooglePlus, Twitter, and Amazon and I solved novel problems that have a practical impact and the solutions often involve the design of new techniques or adapting techniques from various fields such as graph theory, algorithms, statistics, etc.

Google AI Residency has given me the opportunity to collaborate with brilliant researcher on challenging machine learning problems. Many important real-world datasets are in the form of graphs or networks: social networks, knowledge graphs, protein-interaction networks, the World Wide Web, etc. (just to name a few). Most of my current research devoted to the generalization of neural network models to such real-world datasets, where the goal is to exploit the graph structure of such datasets in the training process.

CHwC-HMHqKI.title: Philip Kiely | Keynote: Beyond the Frontier: The economics of the multi-model era

CHwC-HMHqKI.description:
For the last few years, the AI conversation has been dominated by a handful of frontier, closed-weight models but that era is ending. As open-source models have become better and better and new specialized model labs have emerged, the industry is shifting toward a multi-model future. This future is one where open source and closed-weight models are distributed, evaluated, and run side by side on shared infrastructure, and where the right model is chosen on quality and performance for a specific job rather than the lab who created it. Baseten sits at the center of this shift, serving as a hub for distributing both open source and closed-weight models at production scale. In this talk, Philip Kiely, author of Inference Engineering and early employee at Baseten, will make the case for why this shift is not just inevitable but good for the industry. The unit economics of open source models now dramatically outperform frontier models for equivalent tasks, and smaller, fine-tuned models frequently outperform large general-purpose models on quality, latency, and cost for real customer workloads. Drawing on data from production deployments, this talk will show why the future of AI isn't one model for all tasks. It's the right model, for the right job, at the right price.

CdumBT9Jd7A.title: Chetan Conikee: Your agents' traces are your most valuable asset: reading the software factory floor
CdumBT9Jd7A.label: The AI Conference
CdumBT9Jd7A.description:
A modern harness does not click buttons. It writes a shell line, a pipe, an inline script, and hands it to an interpreter. It does that in step with one inference backend, the frontier model it was trained against and benchmarked with. Swap the harness and you have not measured efficiency; you have changed the model, the prompt cache, the tool vocabulary and the compaction rules at once. Olki sits beside the harness you already use—Codex and OpenCode—and records what actually ran. Each line becomes typed events, one per stage, with the program, its arguments, and what it touched. From that record, four readers get their own view: the organization across machines, the inference provider counting repeated failures and the cache that carries the bill, and the product owner asking how agents use the tool they shipped. This session walks the software factory floor: how your harness interacts with the inference provider stack, how a prefix cache lives, why turn two must reach turn one's node, what a subagent or a model switch costs, and what you can only learn by reading the record instead of swapping the harness.

Towards agentic Graph RAG: Combining the power of structured outputs from LLMs with graph databases

In this talk, we will showcase how modern, open source tools like BAML (an AI framework for prompting LLMs to generate structured responses), and Kuzu, an open source embedded graph database, provide developers with the right building blocks to build agentic Graph RAG systems. A common challenge to adopting graphs and graph databases has been the first step: Creating the graph itself.  A lot of data in enterprises is unstructured images or text, and obtaining high-quality knowledge graphs for RAG has historically been a tedious and error prone process. This talk will highlight how to use modular, atomic agentic building blocks that can power the graph construction phase and the retrieval phase, storing the results in a fast, easy-to-use graph database, in order to obtain higher quality knowledge graphs and more reliably generate outputs from Graph RAG systems.

FRT95lDrR5w.description:
Dr.  Rebecca Portnoff, Vice President, Data Science, Thorn

Safety by Design for Generative AI: Preventing Child Sexual Abuse

We are at a crossroads with generative artificial intelligence (generative AI). Generative AI is being misused today to further sexual harm against children. 1 in 10 minors report knowing peers that have used generative AI to create explicit images of other kids; 11% of reports of sexual extortion (in which tactics were apparent) to the National Center of Missing and Exploited Children, included threatening children with fake sexual imagery; 50% of Law Enforcement have encountered AI-generated child sexual abuse material used to groom minors; the Internet Watch Foundation observed a 10% increase in sadistic and hardcore AI-generated child sexual abuse material in the material they assessed from 2023 to 2024.

Yet, we find ourselves in a rare moment — a window of opportunity — to still go down the right path with generative AI and ensure children are protected as the technology is built. In a show of powerful collective action, some of the world’s most influential AI leaders have chosen to do just that. In collaboration with Thorn and All Tech Is Human: Amazon, Anthropic, Civitai, Google, Invoke, Meta, Metaphysic, Microsoft, Mistral AI, OpenAI, and Stability AI have publicly committed to Safety by Design principles. This responsible and ethical AI framework guards against the creation and spread of AI-generated child sexual abuse material (AIG-CSAM) and other sexual harms against children.

This presentation will cover the details of this initiative: how strategy has resulted in impact, how this framework for responsible and ethical AI as it relates to child safety has been adopted globally, and how AI governance and responsible AI professionals can pursue this same impact.

As coding agents get better, the limiting factor is no longer just model capability. It is whether your team has built the right harness around the model: the codebase structure, task boundaries, feedback loops, evals, tests, review processes, and operational guardrails that let agents work effectively over longer time horizons. This talk will cover the emerging shift from pair programming with AI to agentic delegation. It will examine what kinds of engineering work agents handle well today, where they still break down, and what changes teams are making to get useful results in practice. Topics will include how to make a codebase more agent-friendly, how to scope tasks so agents do not thrash, how to use tests and evals as control systems, and how human review changes when the AI is doing more of the implementation work. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for thinking about “harness engineering,” along with concrete patterns they can apply to code review, task design, evals, and team workflows as AI systems take on a larger share of software development.

G2PNv_iNURQ.title: Piyush Agarwal: Introducing Redpanda's Agentic Data Plane
G2PNv_iNURQ.label: The AI Conference
G2PNv_iNURQ.description:
AI agents are increasingly deployed as digital employees—accessing enterprise data, making decisions, and acting autonomously. But agents are both less predictable than humans (prone to hallucination, misinterpretation, and adversarial manipulation) and more capable, with deep system access and machine-speed execution that can cascade damage fast. This makes it unsafe to trust agents to faithfully interpret or propagate security-critical metadata like access policies, data classifications, and behavioral constraints. We present Redpanda's Agentic Data Plane (ADP): an architecture using out-of-band metadata channels that carry security context, policy signals, and audit trails deterministically—entirely outside the agent's read/write path, across heterogeneous infrastructure. These channels enforce governance at every stage of the agent lifecycle: scoping data access going in, constraining actions during execution, and capturing tamper-proof audit trails coming out.

Curtis Northcutt, CEO, Co-Founder, Cleanlab

Practical Strategies with Guarantees for Building Trustworthy Customer-facing AI Support Agents

As customer-facing GenAI support systems move from prototypes to production, reliability is no longer a nice-to-have—it’s a hard requirement. Just ask the teams behind NYC’s MyCity chatbot, which advised businesses to break the law; Air Canada’s support AI refund assistant, which hallucinated non-existent policies and cost the airline real money; or Cursor’s AI-powered support agent, which confidently fabricated a login policy and triggered a wave of user cancellations. These public failures aren’t edge cases. They’re symptoms of a deeper reliability gap in how we build and monitor AI-driven support.
In this session, we’ll explore common failure modes in customer-support GenAI systems—from factual mistakes and hallucinations to deeper reasoning and alignment issues—and walk through practical strategies for detecting and remediating them. We’ll demo how to integrate real-time trustworthiness checks into Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Agentic systems, and show how Cleanlab AI platform can be used to deliver expert-verified, zero-hallucination responses; enforce guardrails for safety, compliance, and helpfulness; surface root-cause insights to diagnose retrieval failures and documentation gaps; and route customer intent to the right support channel. We’ll also discuss how to incorporate human-AI collaboration to strengthen accountability and trust.
If you’re building GenAI customer-support agents that users or businesses rely on, this talk will help you close the gap between promising prototypes and production systems you can stand behind.

GsI39jK6dN0.title: Lindsay Walker | Keynote: Agentic Commerce: Financial, Legal, and End-User Interaction
GsI39jK6dN0.label: The AI Conference
GsI39jK6dN0.description:
Existing payment rails, and all that is built around it, from customer identity verification, to terms of service, to the tools you use to manage and facilitate payments were built with the human user experience in mind. As companies and industries explore the use of AI in commerce, trading, and financial markets, they realize that the traditional systems used to carry out these transactions cannot be easily adapted for use by AI Agents. Companies from Stripe to Coinbase to Cloudflare are recognizing the new capabilities and technologies needed to enable agentic commerce and are building toward that future. The way that you provide and control funds accessible to an agent, as well as how commercial flows like shopping and checkout are executed will need to be redesigned, as adapting human-centric rails doesn’t work in an AI-driven environment. Provisioning a virtual credit card for an agent doesn’t mean that agent will be able to use those funds in most commercial flows. This keynote will explore some of the gaps that exist in using traditional systems with AI, and propose some of the new solutions that can be adopted. Enterprises will understandably need more control compared to a hobby builder to enable secure agentic workflows with commercial transactions, and this keynote will discuss what the future looks like for different parties. With a summary of what is being built and what standards are being developed, this talk will give a high level view of what a commerce-enabled agentic future looks like. Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLTs) are especially well suited to play a role in Agentic Commerce, providing the infrastructure for payments, solidifying and recording human intent, legal agreements, and audit trails for agentic actions.

Dr. Garth Andrus, Global Leader, Digital, AI & Organization Transformation Andersen Consulting

Why Your Organization Is Built to Fail at AI (And What to Do About It): The bold case for rewiring your structure, leadership, and culture to unlock AI’s full potential

AI is not failing because of bad models. It’s failing because it’s being deployed inside organizational models that were never designed for it. While leaders continue to invest in AI, 70–80% of projects still underdeliver—and the real issue isn’t the tech. It’s the structure, the design of work, leadership behaviors, and cultural norms that surround it.
This session exposes a critical blind spot in enterprise AI strategy: most organizations are running AI on top of outdated operating models that actively resist its success. From AI agents stuck in IT silos, to static roles designed for yesterday’s workflows, to leadership mindsets optimized for control—not complexity—today’s companies are mismatched with the nature of AI.
Drawing from research, real-world examples and C-suite experience across Fortune 500 companies, Dr. Garth Andrus makes the case for targeted, pragmatic rewiring—not reinvention—of your organization’s DNA. He’ll share a clear framework to help leaders:
• Diagnose where their organization is quietly blocking AI’s potential
• Shift from job-based design to adaptive, AI-human co-working and collaboration models
• Redesign decision rights, governance, and performance systems to accelerate AI value
• Prepare leadership teams to operate at the intersection of people and machines

Key takeaway: You don’t need a new org chart—you need a rewired operating model. Because in the AI era, the biggest risk isn’t technology failure. It’s leading like nothing has changed.

IuOIVUiE6f8.title: Honpeng Guo, ByteDance: verl: A Flexible and Efficient RL Framework for LLM Reasoning & Tool-calling

IuOIVUiE6f8.description:
Hongpeng Guo, Research Scientist, ByteDance

verl: A Flexible and Efficient RL Framework for LLM Reasoning and Tool-calling

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled advances in language understanding and multimodal tasks, yet scaling reinforcement learning (RL) with these models remains challenging: most existing frameworks either lack the abstractions needed to define and manage complex dataflows or cannot handle models with billions of parameters.
verl (https://github.com/volcengine/verl) is an open-source framework for building end-to-end RL pipelines with LLMs. It provides high-level abstractions and optimizations for dataflow orchestration and resource management via a Ray-based hybrid-controller model. It offers high-level abstractions for dataflow orchestration and resource management: the entire RL dataflow runs as a single controller process on the Ray driver, issuing primitive API calls to WorkerGroup modules. The WorkerGroup and ResourcePool components distribute computation and resources across GPU clusters, delivering high throughput and strong extensibility.
Since its release, verl has seen adoption in both academic research and industry production. It integrates with major training backends (FSDP, FSDP2, Megatron-LM) and inference engines (vLLM, SGLang), and supports various RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, DAPO, etc) with effortless scaling. Recent trends in reasoning models bring new challenges to RL infrastructure, such as efficient tool calling, multi-turn interactions, and capability to scale up to giant MoE models like DeepSeek 671B. To lower the barrier to RL for advanced reasoning and tool calling, we recently improved verl with (1) efficient request level async multi-turn rollout and tool calling, (2) integration with expert parallelism for large scale MoE models, and (3) async system architecture for off-policy / async RL algorithms and flexible device placement.

J-L2jFwNJcU.description:
As AI agents move from demos into production, many teams discover that a more powerful model does not automatically produce better results. The real challenge is often context: giving the agent the right information, at the right time, in the right form. This session shares lessons learned from building and scaling Incident Manager Assist, an enterprise multi-agent system designed to support complex incident investigations. As adoption grew and more enterprise data was connected, we encountered recurring problems: too much information overwhelmed the model, long-running investigations lost important decisions, answers were not tailored to the user, operational data became stale, and expensive models were used even for simple tasks. These challenges led us to six practical context engineering patterns: model-driven control flow, scoped context assembly, intent-driven layered memory, user-aware context, task-adaptive model routing, and continuous context. Attendees will leave with a clear way to think about context, and practical patterns for making context-aware agents reliable in production.

J04YZ7UnVeI.title: Joshua Rubin: Observe, Enforce, and Govern: The Fiddler Control Plane and Centor Models
J04YZ7UnVeI.label: The AI Conference
J04YZ7UnVeI.description:
An agent in your pipeline just wrote code, called an API, or touched a database, and nobody reviewed it first. That's the autonomy agents already have. The question is whether you'd know if one did something wrong, and how long it would take you to find out. That’s what the AI Control Plane is for: a system of trust that starts with evaluation, since that's what makes it possible to monitor an agent's activity, enforce policy on an agent's actions before they execute, and govern behavior across the agentic lifecycle. We'll show what this looks like in practice: inline guardrails that check an agent's actions before they execute, and dashboards that break down exactly what every agent is doing and spending by developer, team, and token. We'll also show how Fiddler Centor Models come batteries-included, no external API calls, no added cost per evaluation, so you can evaluate 100% of your traces or scale down to sampling for smaller deployments. The same approach works whether you're operating a handful of agents or a fleet. You'll leave with a practical way to decide which of your agents have earned more autonomy, and how to give it to them without losing the ability to govern what they're doing.

J6eJbzBUk9w.title: Sergey Levine | Keynote: Robot Foundation Models
J6eJbzBUk9w.label: The AI Conference
J6eJbzBUk9w.description:
Foundation models have transformed how we interact with AI systems. JUWkwVG6Ubs.title: Ion Stoica, Berkeley: Reliability, an AI challenge
JUWkwVG6Ubs.label: The AI Conference
JUWkwVG6Ubs.description:
Ion Stoica, Professor & Executive Chairman, University of California at Berkeley, Anyscale
 
Reliability, an AI challenge

Reliability is a critical obstacle to the successful deployment of AI systems in production. As with conventional software, moving an AI system from prototype to production is far from trivial, requiring robust testing, debugging, and governance. However, unlike conventional systems where components have clear specifications, AI systems—particularly those built on large language models—are black boxes, making failures difficult to detect and diagnose. To address this challenge, we present two systems: LMArena, which evaluates LLMs with real human prompts to measure both accuracy and the impact of style, and MAST, a taxonomy and dataset that reveal why multi-agent systems fail, including poor specifications, misalignment, and weak verification. We argue that achieving reliability requires transforming AI development into a true engineering discipline, grounded in better specifications that are essential for building, debugging, and verifying modular and robust systems.

KJTbr72fsJ8.title: Yuri Shelke: Scaling Enterprise RAG: Distributed Indexing and Dynamic Retrieval at Terabyte Scale
KJTbr72fsJ8.label: The AI Conference
KJTbr72fsJ8.description:
Standard vector search architectures collapse under the weight of indexing latency, ballooning storage costs, and degraded retrieval precision when enterprise RAG systems scale to terabyte-scale production knowledge bases, hitting a Scaling Wall. This session explores the engineering patterns required to build a high-throughput enterprise search infrastructure. Using our production implementation as a case study, we graduate from basic vector stores to a distributed indexing strategy. We will analyze the critical trade-offs between Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) accuracy and memory overhead, the impact of hybrid metadata-vector filtering on query latency, and the necessity of partitioned retrieval architectures to maintain sub-second response times. Attendees will gain a blueprint for a "Knowledge Lake" architecture, learning how to handle incremental indexing at scale, manage vector infrastructure costs, and implement dynamic query routing to ensure system consistency across distributed environments. Key Takeaways: * Distributed Indexing & Sharding: Partition billion-vector datasets across distributed nodes using HNSW/IVF algorithms to ensure sub-second retrieval without exhausting cluster memory. * Trade-off - ANN accuracy vs Memory: Tune ANN indexes for billions of vectors, balancing retrieval speed against infrastructure spend with tiered storage. * Partitioned Retrieval & IVF Strategies: Engineering strategies for segmenting vector space using Inverted File Indexing (IVF), centroid-based sharding, and cluster-level pruning to achieve high search completeness with minimal compute overhead. * Hybrid Filtering & Routing: Implementation patterns for combining structured metadata filters with vector similarity to optimize retrieval performance. * Operational Consistency: Monitoring ingestion lag, managing incremental indexing, and ensuring data integrity across distributed vectors. Engineering Trade-offs & Operational Insights: * Ingestion Scaling vs. Index Freshness: Dynamic task mapping in Airflow and Spark to parallelize the embedding bottleneck while managing vector database write-limits. * Vector Storage Economics: Reducing high-dimensionality embeddings cost through product quantization (PQ) and binary hashing. * System Resiliency: Handling retrieval hot spots and implementing circuit breakers for bulk data backfills that threaten to saturate vector endpoints.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

Brain icon for The AI Conference 2023, a groundbreaking two-day event on AGI, LLMs, Infrastructure, Alignment, AI Startups, and Neural Architectures.

Agentic AI for Financial Data: Automating Insights from Large-Scale Tables

1. Problem Statement: Financial datasets are vast, complex, and difficult to process manually. Extracting key insights from large financial tables remains a bottleneck for analysts. Unlike free-form text, tabular data is hierarchical, relational, and context-dependent, requiring specialized techniques for accurate summarization and insight generation. Traditional LLMs struggle with numerical reasoning, row-column relationships, and multi-step financial calculations, making agentic AI architectures essential for structured data interpretation. 2. Agentic AI Approach: Built an autonomous AI agent leveraging LLMs and domain-specific fine-tuning to analyze, summarize, and extract key financial insights dynamically. 3. Core Capabilities:    a. LLM Fine-Tuning: Trained on financial documents to improve context understanding and numerical reasoning.      i. Bayesian Optimization for hyperparameter tuning.      ii.Contrastive Learning to improve structured data representation.      iii.Quantile Regression to enhance financial trend prediction.      iv. Expectation-Maximization (EM) for better handling of missing data in tabular structures. b. Named Entity Recognition (NER) & Ontology Learning:      i. Developed a NER model to learn the ontology of financial use cases, enabling precise identification of different columns and their        relationships.    ii. Fine-tuned an embedding model to capture semantic relationships between financial entities, improving contextual understanding        of structured data.   c. Evaluation Framework: Supports researchers in assessing different prompting techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Chain-of-Table (CoTab) to improve reasoning on structured financial data.    d. Tabular Data Extraction: AI pipeline identifies patterns, trends, and anomalies in financial statements.    e. Synthetic Data Generation: Capable of creating synthetic financial datasets for benchmarking, evaluation, and fine-tuning the framework.   f. Explainability & Auditability: Ensures AI-generated insights are traceable and interpretable for decision-makers.  4. Impact & Business Value:     a. Efficiency Gains: Reduces manual processing time from hours to minutes.     b. Enhanced Decision-Making: Empowers financial professionals with concise, data-driven summaries.     c. Scalability: Adaptable across different financial reports, including earnings statements, balance sheets, and regulatory filings. Conclusion: This agentic AI architecture bridges the gap between raw financial data and actionable intelligence, offering a research-friendly framework for advancing structured reasoning in AI. By addressing the unique complexities of tabular financial data, it enables more accurate, interpretable, and scalable AI-driven financial analysis.

L52bqXMtLgI.title: Jonathan Nolen & Timothy Cook: Controlling AI Software Factories: Engineers in Charge at Agent Speed

L52bqXMtLgI.description:
AI is not just changing how fast software is written. It is changing how software is produced.  Engineering organizations are assembling agent-powered systems that write code, review pull requests, validate releases, deploy changes, and continuously improve production software around the clock, without human hands on every step. The promise of faster software delivery and continuous optimization is real. But as delivery becomes more autonomous, a new and more urgent problem surfaces: how do you stay in control of systems that never stop evolving? In this session, Jonathan Nolen, Chief Product Officer at LaunchDarkly, makes the case that the defining challenge of the AI era is not generating code — it is controlling autonomous systems in production. Traditional pre-production controls and the standard playbook of detect, fix, redeploy break down for agents that don't fail like traditional software. They drift. You can no longer catch issues before production. You have to control production. Jonathan will share what LaunchDarkly has learned building its own AI software factory — including what happened when coding agents met its oldest, most complex production code — and why every autonomous delivery system requires a closed control loop: observation, decision-making, intervention, and feedback, all running at runtime without a deploy cycle. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for building AI software factories that are genuinely fast and safe, and a clear answer to the question every engineering leader is now facing: when agents are doing the work, who stays in charge?

Discover how Clockwork’s edge-based congestion control technology can turbocharge NCCL communication throughput by 2.6x on TCP/IP+Ethernet networks, which can significantly shorten the time needed for LLM training on such networks.

Brain icon for The AI Conference 2023, a groundbreaking two-day event on AGI, LLMs, Infrastructure, Alignment, AI Startups, and Neural Architectures.Based on foundational clock sync technology developed at Stanford University, Clockwork’s software can transform unpredictable data networks into deterministic, time-sensitive systems. In this talk, we’ll provide an in-depth look at Packet Rocket—-an easy-to-deploy software solution that can enable TCP+Ethernet networks to deliver 100% utilization at near-zero packet loss. We will also present results from NCCL tests and discuss how the technology can be used to improve the performance of LLM workloads on TCP+Ethernet networks without hardware support or upgrades.

About Vinay Sriram
Vinay Sriram is a senior software engineer at Clockwork Systems. His recent work studies the benefit of Clockwork's foundational congestion control technology on machine learning workloads in the public cloud. Vinay also works on Clockwork’s real-time network monitoring and clock synchronization solutions. He holds a B.S. and M.S. in computer science from Stanford University. Before joining Clockwork, he was a research assistant in the Stanford Platform Lab, and has worked on ML teams at Google and Amazon.

Data starved? Let’s feed the models.

“We’re running out of data” has become a common concern among AI developers. In this session, Jessica Li Gebert, data strategist at Neudata, challenges that perception - highlighting how data leaders are overlooking high-quality data assets stored behind corporate firewalls. This session is for AI developers who seek high-quality training data and organization that may be sitting on valuable datasets without a clear path to monetization. Jessica introduces the growing ecosystem of  AI data licensing - a practical ecosystem where companies can safely monetize their internal data and AI developers can gain access to the specialized datasets they need for innovation. Jessica posits that the current challenge is not true scarcity; rather, the challenge lies in bridging the gap between companies that own valuable datasets and AI developers who urgently need them. As public data sources have become depleted, and web-scraping becomes costlier and more restricted, we’ll look at how enterprises across sectors such as finance, healthcare, media, logistics or retail possess substantial reserves of data. Originally captured for regulatory compliance, business intelligence or marketing, these assets hold enormous untapped potential for training AI models. Drawing on extensive project experience, and unpacking well-known licensing deals, Jessica will clearly outline the current market landscape and: How enterprises can responsibly commercialize underutilized data assets Best practices and strategic frameworks for successful data licensing How AI developers can ethically and effectively source datasets Ways to overcome common barriers and accelerate mutually beneficial partnerships Real-world insights and strategic considerations for long-term success Join this practical session if your organization is exploring the opportunities that lie in the gap between perceived data scarcity and the reality of underutilized corporate datasets. Learn how data owners and AI innovators can partner effectively and turn dormant data assets into strategic, sustainable opportunities for growth.

How to Build a Multimodal Data Lake: Unlocking the Next Generation of AI Workloads

While the model stack has evolved rapidly to reason across images, text, audio, and video, most data stacks are still catching up. Traditional data engines like Spark and Trino are designed and optimized for structured, tabular data and not for unstructured data and rich media like images and audio – falling short for the needs of multimodal data in today’s workloads.


In this talk, we explore what it means to build a multimodal data lake designed to handle demands of modern AI workloads, such as heterogeneous datasets spanning images, text, and tabular data, allowing teams to unlock new ML/AI capabilities without being limited by traditional, tabular-only systems. We’ll dive into the architectural patterns behind Daft, an open-source Python-native unified data engine purpose-built for modern AI/ML data workflows, that allow for efficient and scalable data processing across modalities.


We’ll walk through:
- Why traditional data lakes fail in multimodal settings
- Concrete design patterns for building efficient, scalable multimodal ETL pipelines without blowing out memory or compute resources
- How to query multimodal datasets interactively, using a familiar SQL or Python DataFrame API


Join us as we demonstrate how to build a multimodal data lake using Daft on your existing infrastructure. Your data layer should be flexible enough for experimentation and also powerful enough to scale.

Open source and open science in generative AI have advanced greatly in the past 2 years, with open capabilities now approaching parity with proprietary systems, and a flourishing researcher and developer ecosystem innovating across the stack, from new tuning methods to infrastructure optimizations to agentic application frameworks and beyond. Still, there is a lot to do: from domain-specific safety and evaluation of AI systems, to democratizing methods of tuning, to ensuring highly capable open models can be integrated and deployed efficiently in a variety of use cases and contexts. The enterprise perspective is especially illuminating, where almost all large companies have targets to adopt generative AI, but where the divide between proof of concept and production is often still large.

I’ll present a perspective on the path ahead to achieve widespread adoption of generative AI in companies and how IBM’s open source AI contributions and the AI Alliance of more than 100 leading AI technology and research organizations are enabling this path.

OykNwu0unAA.title: Priyambada Jain, Black Rock: Agentic AI for Financial Data
OykNwu0unAA.label: The AI Conference
OykNwu0unAA.description:
Priyambada Jain, Senior Data Scientist, BlackRock

Agentic AI for Financial Data: Automating Insights from Large-Scale Tables

1. Problem Statement: Financial datasets are vast, complex, and difficult to process manually. Extracting key insights from large financial tables remains a bottleneck for analysts. Unlike free-form text, tabular data is hierarchical, relational, and context-dependent, requiring specialized techniques for accurate summarization and insight generation. Traditional LLMs struggle with numerical reasoning, row-column relationships, and multi-step financial calculations, making agentic AI architectures essential for structured data interpretation. 2. Agentic AI Approach: Built an autonomous AI agent leveraging LLMs and domain-specific fine-tuning to analyze, summarize, and extract key financial insights dynamically. 3. Core Capabilities:    a. LLM Fine-Tuning: Trained on financial documents to improve context understanding and numerical reasoning.      i. Bayesian Optimization for hyperparameter tuning.      ii.Contrastive Learning to improve structured data representation.      iii.Quantile Regression to enhance financial trend prediction.      iv. Expectation-Maximization (EM) for better handling of missing data in tabular structures. b. Named Entity Recognition (NER) & Ontology Learning:      i. Developed a NER model to learn the ontology of financial use cases, enabling precise identification of different columns and their        relationships.    ii. Fine-tuned an embedding model to capture semantic relationships between financial entities, improving contextual understanding        of structured data.   c. Evaluation Framework: Supports researchers in assessing different prompting techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Chain-of-Table (CoTab) to improve reasoning on structured financial data.    d. Tabular Data Extraction: AI pipeline identifies patterns, trends, and anomalies in financial statements.    e. Synthetic Data Generation: Capable of creating synthetic financial datasets for benchmarking, evaluation, and fine-tuning the framework.   f. Explainability & Auditability: Ensures AI-generated insights are traceable and interpretable for decision-makers.  4. Impact & Business Value:     a. Efficiency Gains: Reduces manual processing time from hours to minutes.     b. Enhanced Decision-Making: Empowers financial professionals with concise, data-driven summaries.     c. Scalability: Adaptable across different financial reports, including earnings statements, balance sheets, and regulatory filings. Conclusion: This agentic AI architecture bridges the gap between raw financial data and actionable intelligence, offering a research-friendly framework for advancing structured reasoning in AI. By addressing the unique complexities of tabular financial data, it enables more accurate, interpretable, and scalable AI-driven financial analysis.

Q7-oKuXxx5w.title: Adrian Kosowski | Keynote: Post-Transformer Frontier: More Intelligence per Watt, Token & Dollar
Q7-oKuXxx5w.label: The AI Conference
Q7-oKuXxx5w.description:
Transformers have reshaped AI, but they were never designed as a foundation for intelligence that must persist and grow over time. Today’s reasoning models often gain capability by generating and accumulating an ever-growing trace of reasoning tokens. This raises latency, drives up inference cost, and increases energy consumption. We are already seeing diminishing returns from scaling parameters and inference-time compute. This keynote explains why the next frontier in AI will come from architectural breakthroughs that produce more intelligence per watt, token, and dollar. I will map the emerging post-Transformer landscape across three architectural frontiers: persistent and recurrent memory, sparse and selective computation, and continual adaptation — and show how they need to come together to achieve this goal. I will then introduce BDH — an architecture that unifies memory, reasoning, and adaptation — and lay out a path beyond static parameters and ephemeral token histories toward AI systems that retain what matters, reason and adapt over long horizons, and improve through experience.

Jisheng Wang, VP Engineering and Head of AI/ML, Traceable

Securing the New Attack Surface:Navigating the Security Risks and Protection of LLMs

Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a cornerstone technology, reshaping every industry and revolutionizing how we interact with digital systems. Much like the advent of network computing and cloud technology before it, the widespread adoption of LLMs heralds a new era of innovation and, with it, a novel attack surface ripe for exploitation. This talk aims to shed light on the inherent security risks associated with LLMs with the real-world examples of LLM-targeted exploitation, and emphasize the importance of proactive threat management in safeguarding the future of LLM-driven applications. Since LLMs will be widely used in future applications, we will first give an overview of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 Application Risks and Top 10 API Risks which are still applicable to LLMs. Next we will focus on the OWASP Top 10 LLM Specific Risks, and delve into three detailed examples of Prompt Injection, Sensitive Information Disclosure, and Training Data Poisoning. Each example is accompanied by a demonstration of the potential for exploitation, and also the strategies for mitigating these threats and protecting against attacks.

The goal of this talk is to educate the broad AI developer community with the potential risks and vulnerabilities of LLMs and also the knowledge to protect against them, and foster a culture of security that keeps pace with the rapid advancements in AI technology.

QvVXiJv39aY.description:
Most AI applications today rely on cloud inference, which introduces latency, privacy concerns, operational cost, and limits real-time interactivity. In games, these constraints are especially problematic: player experiences must respond instantly and scale to millions of users without bankrupting developers. In this talk, we present the architecture and production lessons behind Bobium Brawlers, the first mobile game that runs generative AI entirely on device. The system powers real-time creature and gameplay content generation without a deluge of cloud API calls. We will walk through the design of a production system capable of running generative models locally on consumer devices, including: Designing gameplay systems around local LLM and generative model inference Techniques for model compression, optimization, and quality Integrating AI generation directly into core gameplay loops rather than cosmetic features Handling latency, guardrails and reliability when inference happens inside the game Lessons learned from deploying the system to real players and observing emergent gameplay We will also discuss how AI-native design changes traditional game development workflows, including content pipelines, player creativity systems, and balancing mechanics when AI becomes part of the game itself. Attendees will walk away with practical insights into shipping AI-first interactive systems on constrained devices, including architectural patterns, optimization strategies, and lessons from deploying generative AI in a live product.

RGHcY65GlBE.title: Deepti Srivastava: Data Architectures in the Age of AI: Rebuilding Data Stacks for Autonomous Agents
RGHcY65GlBE.label: The AI Conference
RGHcY65GlBE.description:
Every major computing shift has reshaped the software stack, but one assumption held across all of them: humans were the primary consumers of software and software-generated artifacts. AI agents break this assumption. An autonomous agent determines at runtime what data it needs, interprets it, and takes actions, with no human in the loop to catch misinterpretations. In this new era, bolting AI features onto existing app-centric, or warehouse- and lakehouse-centric stacks just isn't enough to meet the requirements of these agents. The data layer must be rethought from first principles to enable agents to run critical decision-making workflows using structured operational data, reliably and with confidence. In this talk, I’ll discuss three imperative changes – automatically generated and maintained business semantics, federation as the default retrieval path, and governance – and show how our new agent-native data platform incorporates these principles.

Re_ed73Un3w.description:
Josh Rubin, Principal AI Scientist, Fiddler AI

AI All the Way Down: Building Trust into Generative Applications with Model-Based Feedback

Generative AI promises to unlock unprecedented efficiency and enhance human expertise in collaborative workflows. However, this technology differs from predictive AI in significant ways, and that creates new challenges to safety and reliability. One important difference is that unlike their predictive predecessors, LLMs are trained on general purpose tasks and subsequently applied to different, specific problem spaces. This means that gathering performance feedback and root-causing problems is not as simple as comparing a prediction against a ground-truth label.

In this talk, we’ll explore closing the feedback loop for generative applications with model-based metrics. At Fiddler AI, we call them “Trust Models” and they’re used both for offline diagnostics and synchronous runtime-path use cases where unsafe or underperforming output is intercepted in real-time.

Beyond Text Generation: The Rise of Agentic AI and Its Transformative Potential

The evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) from reactive text generators to proactive autonomous agents represents one of the most significant paradigm shifts in artificial intelligence. This presentation explores how agentic AI systems—capable of goal-directed behavior, environmental interaction, and decision autonomy—are redefining human-AI collaboration across industries. Drawing on recent research, we'll examine the technical foundations enabling this transformation: hierarchical planning structures, long-term memory architectures, and tool integration frameworks that dramatically enhance performance on complex tasks. The discussion will cover contrasting operational frameworks like ReAct, which demonstrates significantly higher completion rates on benchmark tasks, and Plan-and-Execute approaches, which receive stronger stakeholder ratings for internal consistency. We'll address critical ethical considerations including the Graduated Autonomy Framework, which reduces intervention requirements while maintaining safety, and explore cutting-edge developments in multi-agent systems, embodied agency, continual learning, and meta-learning—where adaptive architectures require fewer examples to master novel tasks. With hundreds of research papers published on novel agent architectures in recent years, agentic AI represents the frontier of artificial intelligence research and application. This presentation provides a comprehensive overview of current capabilities, emerging challenges, and future directions for practitioners and decision-makers navigating this rapidly evolving landscape.

SWdcSCRYhds.title: Brian Joe: Runtime is Where AI Lives
SWdcSCRYhds.label: The AI Conference
SWdcSCRYhds.description:
Your AI stack didn't add a new application. It added a newparticipant. Agents now make calls, invoke tools, read untrusted content, and act on your systems with credentials of their own — and almost all of it happens at Layer 7, in runtime, where your existing controls were never designed to look. AI opened four new doors at once: autonomous agents, prompt injection, the model supply chain, and identity sprawl. Meanwhile attackers do what they've always done — move across identity, apps, APIs, data, and infrastructure without respecting the tool boundaries we bought. This session makes the case that runtime is becoming the control plane for modern security, and shows what that actually changes day to day: vulnerability management driven by what's exposed and reachable instead of a CVSS backlog; detection built on behavior instead of static signatures; and the shift frompanic patchtorapid protection— reduce risk now, patch on your timeline. Brian Joe, CPO and co-founder of Impart Security, will walk through the four AI threat vectors, the unified runtime view, and a practical picture of SecOps in the AI era.

Physical AI integrates artificial intelligence with physical systems, enabling machines to interact seamlessly with the real world in a virtual environment, enhancing sectors such as robotics and autonomous driving. However, developing Physical AI presents significant challenges, including ensuring systems accurately replicate real-world diversity, necessitating ongoing refinement and validation.​

NVIDIA's Cosmos World Foundation Models (WFMs) address these challenges by providing pre-trained models that simulate real-world physics, enabling developers to create AI systems capable of understanding and interacting with the physical world, leading to more efficient and intelligent solutions. Complementing COSMOS, the NeMo Framework simplifies the customization of these models to meet specific needs, allowing developers to fine-tune AI applications for improved performance, broadening the scope of AI solutions. 

​By integrating NVIDIA's Cosmos World Foundation Models and the NeMo Framework, developers can accelerate the creation of AI systems that understand complex physical interactions and adapt to diverse applications, revolutionizing robotics and autonomous driving while enhancing innovation and efficiency across industries.
