X9vJSiWSzVY.title: Di Jin: Post-training Is the New Product Moat: Why the Application Layer Trains Its Own Models
X9vJSiWSzVY.label: The AI Conference
X9vJSiWSzVY.description:
Two years ago, post-training was a research term and a checkbox on an inference bill. Today Cursor, Cognition, Harvey and others ship their own models, built on open weights and sharpened with reinforcement learning — not because they wanted to become model labs, but because prompting a general model was no longer good enough for their products. This talk traces how that shift happened and what it means for anyone building AI products. I'll cover the four preconditions that made it possible: open-weight models good enough to specialize, verifiable rewards that made RL practical outside a lab, agents that raised the bar from plausible answers to reliable task completion, and the economics of a small custom model beating a frontier API. I'll then look at how the vendor landscape has organized itself — who sells post-training today, and how much of the work each option leaves in your hands. Drawing on post-training Llama 3 and 4 at Meta, co-founding Eigen AI, and now leading AI training at Nebius, I'll share how we approach this at Nebius: an AI cloud where training tooling — both our own and our partners' — sits directly on the compute, so teams can post-train their own models without stitching together a stack. I'll ground this in a recent customer case and close with three predictions about where post-training goes next.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

_PywBUzxM2s.title: Simeon Bochev, Compute Exchange: AI is still killing innovation
_PywBUzxM2s.label: The AI Conference
_PywBUzxM2s.description:
Simeon Bochev, Co-founder & CEO, Compute Exchange

AI is still killing innovation

It sounds like a contradiction, but it’s not a suggestion that AI itself is doing the damage. Rather, it's the exponentially growing demand for compute – the raw infrastructure that powers AI – and the lack of equitable access to that essential resource. In other words: no compute means no innovation for far too many organizations, large and small. That has to change.
The system for buying compute doesn’t compute. Neither does the lack of market transparency, vendor lock-in, juggling multiple vendors, unused capacity, and heterogeneity. The reality is that most compute buyers are flying blind. There’s no real market price – access to the same GPU service can range from $1.58-$8.50 per hour. When a buyer is able to secure access, there’s no way of knowing whether or not it’s a good deal, or if the technology will even work. 
This presentation will make the case for the commoditization of raw computing power, which could be transformative for fair and equal access. The innate properties of compute naturally lend themselves to standardization and liquid markets: Compute exhibits uniformity as AI's foundational infrastructure, much like electricity in power transmission. It represents an essential raw material for model development, commanding a massive market with capital expenditures in the trillions. Compute also demonstrates minimal differentiation in core capabilities across providers.

Most agents don’t fail in production because the model is bad. They fail because the system around the model has no guardrails, no structure, and no way to see what’s happening. Text Revision with Large Language Models -- Challenges and Opportunities

Text revision is a complex, iterative process. It is no surprise that human writers are unable to simultaneously comprehend multiple demands and constraints of the task of text revision when producing well-written texts, as they are required to cover the content, follow linguistic norms, set the right tone, follow discourse conventions, etc. This presents a massive challenge and opportunity for intelligent writing assistants, which have undergone an enormous shift in their abilities in the past few years and months via large language models and human-feedback learning. In addition to the quality of editing suggestions, writing assistance has undergone a monumental shift in terms of being prescriptive systems to being human-feedback-driven, collaborative systems. However, writing assistants still lack in terms of their quality, personalization, and overall usability, limiting the value they provide to users.

In this talk, I will present my research, challenges, and insights on building intelligent and interactive writing assistants for effective communication and navigating challenges pertaining to quality, personalization, and usability.

ahXQcCZr3ME.title: Dr. Rodney Brooks, Robust AI: Getting Robots Deployed at Scale; Robot Demo Videos Are Not Sufficient
ahXQcCZr3ME.label: The AI Conference
ahXQcCZr3ME.description:
Dr. Rodney Brooks, Co-founder & CTO, Robust AI

Getting Robots Deployed at Scale; Robot Demo Videos Are Not Sufficient

It is a golden age for robotics, driven by amazing amounts of compute available onboard, low cost hardware driven by smartphones, electric scooters, and smart appliances, and sixty years of AI advances.  And it is a time where robots are desperately needed as labor is short in manufacturing, warehouse/fulfilment, farming, construction, and many other industries.

Rodney Brooks has been a pioneer in robotics and AI in both academia and in six startups over the last 40+ years. His companies have shipped more robots than any others, and in four major product lines. Now at Robust.AI he and his teammates have developed a new class of mobile robots, driven by AI advances, that radically increase the productivity  of people employed in warehouses and manufacturing, by becoming their most valued tools and making their work much less physically demanding.

AI systems have to satisfy human users. Robots do too, but first they have to satisfy physics, and that is a much less forgiving requirement.  Brooks will explain how critical a physics based understanding of robots is to figuring out what it is they need to know about the world, and what they can learn from the world.  And he will lead you through what parts of that are long understood, what parts have just become possible to deploy with reliability, and what parts are still distant dreams.

Finally he will talk about why every physical robot class, from fully autonomous automobiles to home robot vacuums, has a much longer deployment ramp than products which are shipped over the network as ephemeral bits; ranging from reliability of operation, to supply chain vulnerability, to the costs of both underutilized or unavailable inventory.

Key Takeaways:
The evolving role of robots in reshoring U.S. manufacturing and warehouse operations.
How robots are already augmenting human workers in warehouses and what’s next for AI-powered automation.
Practical insights into deploying hybrid automation models to address labor shortages and improve operational efficiency.
Realistic timelines for fully automated warehouses and the gradual shift to more collaborative systems.

am7eqeZ6qWI.description:
Generative AI, Enterprise LLMs And Path To Trillion Parameter Models, Urmish Thakker, SambaNova Systems

Open source LLMs like LLAMA2 and BLOOM have enabled widespread development of enterprise LLM Applications. However, open source LLMs can sometimes lag behind proprietary models. In this talk, we will explore the work done by SambaNova Systems to reduce the gap between open source LLMs and proprietary models. We look into multilingual chat capabilities of BLOOM-176B and how they can be improved, reducing the gap in software API manipulation capabilities of popular open source models and improving long sequence capabilities of existing models. This work and its artifacts (models, benchmarks etc) have been released on HuggingFace for the community to use, evaluate and improve further.

Brain icon for The AI Conference 2023, a groundbreaking two-day event on AGI, LLMs, Infrastructure, Alignment, AI Startups, and Neural Architectures.In our journey of working with our customers to make open source LLMs enterprise ready, we noticed a trend where organizations had a need for both general LLMs and specialized expert LLMs. These expert LLMs are useful in various use cases and scenarios – specialized tasks, context distillation, domain adaptation or incorporating private data. Depending on the complexity of the task, multiple such experts need to come together. However, running them efficiently can be prohibitively expensive. Even with 15 experts at 70b scale, the number of total parameters to hold during inference can easily add up to trillion. We look at how SN40L with its unique hierarchical memory architecture enables faster serving of such a collection of experts, outperforming existing ML hardware providers.

About Urmish Thakker
Urmish leads the NLP Team at SambaNova Systems. The NLP team at SambaNova focuses on understanding how to train and evaluate HHH aligned large language models, adapting LLMs to enterprise use-cases and HW-SW co-design of LLMs to enable efficient training and inference. Before SambaNova, he was in various engineering and research roles at Arm, AMD and Texas Instruments. He also helped drive the TinyML Performance Working Group in MLPerf, contributing to the development of key benchmarks for IoT ML. Urmish has 35+ publications and patents focussing on efficient deep learning and LLMs and has given guest lectures at various top universities and industry academia summits. He completed his masters at the University of Wisconsin Madison and his bachelors from Birla Institute of Technology and Science.

bTnjn7l8bWM.title: Zairah Mustahsan: Measuring What Matters: Statistical Rigor in AI Accuracy Evaluations
bTnjn7l8bWM.label: The AI Conference
bTnjn7l8bWM.description:
Most teams evaluate AI accuracy by running a handful of test queries, picking whichever system looks best, and shipping. The problem is that ad-hoc testing doesn't reflect production behavior and isn't replicable; worse, standard benchmarks aren't calibrated to specific use cases. When you're making infrastructure decisions that cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, cherry-picked demos are not a measurement strategy. This talk introduces a rigorous framework for evaluating AI search quality that applies classical ML statistical principles to a problem the industry has largely treated as subjective. I’ll cover how to construct a golden test set that actually predicts production performance, how to validate LLMs-as-judge against human raters before trusting them at scale, and how to run controlled comparisons across providers. The deeper argument is about what most evaluations get wrong at the measurement level. LLM-based evaluation is inherently stochastic, so the same query, run through the same system, produces different outputs across trials. Reporting accuracy alone can't tell you whether a performance difference is real or just noise; I’ll explain how to decompose evaluation variance into signal and instability. You’ll leave with a methodology you can apply immediately to your own vendor comparisons and internal eval pipelines.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

eBbkbkl2oME.description:
Cooking With The Semantic Kernel: Recipes For Building Chatbots, Agents, And More With Large Language Models

In the short time that large language models have gone mainstream, we’ve started to see several patterns that AI researchers and developers have used to build their products. These include things like prompt engineering, prompt templating, chain of thought, vectorized memory and embeddings, and more. They’ve enabled new forms of natural language-based apps and have truly opened people’s imagination to what is possible with AI.

Brain icon for The AI Conference 2023, a groundbreaking two-day event on AGI, LLMs, Infrastructure, Alignment, AI Startups, and Neural Architectures.This presentation will cover a few of these recipes and how to build them using the Semantic Kernel, Microsoft’s latest open-source framework for developing AI and large language model applications. The Semantic Kernel incorporates the design patterns from the latest in AI research, and provides a multilingual SDK that developers can use to empower their apps with recursive reasoning, contextual memory, semantic indexing, planning, retrieval-augmented generation, and more. Come cook with us!

About Alex Chao
Currently, I’m building next-generation AI products at Microsoft through the Office of the CTO with an emphasis on multimodal and large language models.

Over the last decade, I’ve successfully launched applied ML products across industries in health, gaming, finance, defense, energy, autonomous vehicles, semiconductors, and enterprise tech.

I’ve held product management roles at SambaNova Systems and C3.ai building out ML Platforms and deep learning offerings to enterprise customers. I continue to be an active ML practitioner and was the first data science hire at Uber’s Advanced Technologies Group working on building large scale computer vision and sensor fusion algorithms for self-driving cars.

I’m motivated to help raise the next generation of data scientists and product leaders and have taught and mentored at places like General Assembly, Springboard, and Product School to equip students for their future success. Proud alum of UC Berkeley! Go Bears!

eC0gKKFa-1M.title: Emmanuel Ameisen | Keynote: Language Models, Inside Out: Finding world models hidden in the weights
eC0gKKFa-1M.label: The AI Conference
eC0gKKFa-1M.description:
Language models are superhuman text predictors. The best way to predict a piece of text is to build a rich model of the world that generated it. Look inside a language model and that's what you find: concepts shared across languages and modalities, plans formed well in advance of being enacted, and even evolved algorithms for arithmetic. Prediction, done well enough, becomes simulation. To guess the next word, the model learns to represent the hidden variables behind the text: a speaker's emotions, beliefs, and goals. The field of interpretability has spent the last few years decoding language model weights directly. This talk is a tour of some of the most important findings from this work, and of the mental model they add up to: a language model as a world model, hiding in plain sight in the weights.

g-upPybdXQU.title: Dr. June Andrews, Lat Long Labs: Optimizing Quality of Life:A Feat of Brute Force and Ignorance
g-upPybdXQU.label: The AI Conference
g-upPybdXQU.description:
Dr. June Andrews, Founder, Lat Long Labs

Optimizing Quality of Life:A Feat of Brute Force and Ignorance

Lat Long Labs (LLL) presents the first of its kind – a platform for optimizing quality of life as a function of location and family. In this talk, we will dive into the technology enabling this breakthrough—a constraint optimization machine running over a multi-grid feature space that unifies hundreds of maps covering the eight dimensions influencing quality of life: wealth, employment, environment, health, education, recreation, community, and safety. These maps are personalized to family structure, zip code, occupation, and personal interests for all locations in the United States. All together, LLL produces one step closer to data science + machine learning + AI achieving the zenith of what tech can offer us: to optimize the quality of life for every family—every individual—every human heartbeat.

Optimizing quality of life is such a daunting task it can only be embarked upon with brute force and ignorance, until enough building blocks are in place for clever optimization algorithms to take over. LLL’s initial building block was the development of a personalized total tax model encoding thousands of tax laws. It was then augmented with a personalized income estimator and continually refined until achieving the first of its kind – a personalized discretionary income model – calculating generation of wealth as a function of family and location. Mastering personalized financial models is critical to making actionable recommendations. The additional seven dimensions similarly had models developed from basic building blocks to novel representations. Finally, using a technique from mathematical optimization, constrained optimization, good at handling high dimensional spaces with soft penalty functions, a global optimization is possible for quality of life as a function of location and family.

This talk introduces the architecture underpinning the first known model for simulating and optimizing quality of life as a function of location and family. From this model we show a series of case studies linking the theoretical results of the LLL model with real-life challenges and outcomes for families navigating the dynamic landscape of the United States.

g1tDyIWQPJw.title: Jeremy Adams: Experience Is Abundant. Knowledge Is Distilled.
g1tDyIWQPJw.label: The AI Conference
g1tDyIWQPJw.description:
Generative AI gave us an abundance of content. Agentic AI is giving us something potentially more valuable, while also much more overwhelming: experience. Every tool call, coding session, workflow, decision, observation, and robot trajectory leaves behind another trace of what happened, what worked, and what didn't. But accumulating raw piles of experience isn't the same as learning from it. This talk explores an emerging layer in AI systems devoted not simply to storing context, but to distilling experience into durable, reusable knowledge. We'll connect ideas appearing across agent memory, semantic layers, knowledge bases, coding agents, context graphs, and even physical AI: resolving repeated observations into entities, discovering relationships and patterns, turning trajectories into reusable skills, and feeding what we've learned back into future action. A number of knowledge primitives are competing for this layer, from the humble Markdown document and hypertext to vector embeddings, model weights, and knowledge graphs. Graphs, in particular, keep popping up. They may occupy a sweet spot: knowledge that is structured yet flexible, explicit and inspectable, portable across models and agent harnesses, and capable of generating other representations without surrendering the underlying structure. We'll pressure-test that claim, asking when the graph is useful, when it isn't, and whether increasingly capable models might eventually swallow the whole thing. The last wave of AI was about generation. The next frontier may be about accumulation: building systems that don't just produce more experience, but get better at distilling what it means.

gOpgoHRpbQY.title: Dr. Samantha T. Arundel, U.S. Geological Survey: An Intelligent National Map
gOpgoHRpbQY.label: The AI Conference
gOpgoHRpbQY.description:
Dr. Samantha T. Arundel, Senior Science Advisor, National Geospatial Program, U.S. Geological Survey

An Intelligent National Map: Coordinating Structured Analysis and Scientific Validation Across Authoritative Geospatial Data

The U.S. Geological Survey’s National Map provides a consistent, authoritative foundation for elevation, hydrography, transportation, and land cover data across the United States. However, the increasing complexity of spatial problems has outpaced platforms built around static layer access or manual analysis. An Intelligent National Map (INM) is being developed as a modular framework that supports structured queries, coordinated model workflows, and transparent review of analytic results. Rather than serving as a single tool, an INM organizes existing federal datasets into reusable workflows that support spatial reasoning and policy-relevant analysis.
Each workflow is initiated through a user query and proceeds through configured steps for data retrieval, transformation, modeling, and review. All inputs are drawn directly from agency-maintained sources, including the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), the National Hydrography Dataset (NHD), and land cover datasets such as LCMAP. Results are tied to specific records and returned with complete provenance documentation. Instead of replicating or warehousing data, an INM issues structured queries against live repositories using defined interfaces and schema constraints.
Workflows are carried out by task-specific agents, each aligned to a discrete operation such as model selection, input filtering, or threshold evaluation. Validation is handled by agents configured to compare analytic outputs to published values, ScienceBase records, or ontologically defined spatial relationships. For example, a workflow to delineate flood exposure may combine current stream gauge data with elevation derivatives and surface connectivity metrics to identify risk zones, which are then checked for agreement with hazard maps or published thresholds.
The platform supports use cases in hazard response, infrastructure planning, and environmental monitoring. Examples include wetland persistence mapping based on hydrologic connectivity, optimization of transportation alignments using topographic cost surfaces, and comparison of projected land cover scenarios for zoning evaluation. Results are returned as standardized spatial products along with intermediate diagnostics that document key parameter choices and processing steps.
Every analysis includes a structured explanation layer. Users can view variable contributions, input sources, and references checked by validation agents. Review modules simulate internal steps used in USGS publication workflows, including peer review and policy compliance checks. These are configured using synthetic review personas aligned to the USGS Fundamental Science Practices framework.
Initial development is focused on elevation and hydrography workflows where classification methods and source data are stable. Ongoing work includes refining query interpretation, extending validation loops, and establishing audit mechanisms consistent with governance guidance from the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Long-term planning includes cross-domain integration and federation across federal organizations.

hhym1IJrDUM.description:
Wil Pong, VP of Product, Fiddler

Guardians of Agentic AI: Control Planes for Orchestration and Governance 

The adoption of multi-agent AI systems is transforming governance and compliance, but it also introduces risks that conventional monitoring cannot detect. Autonomous agents communicate, delegate tasks, and chain reasoning in ways that create invisible failure modes and policy violations.

AI control planes act as a guardian layer for these systems, combining observability, guardrails, and governance into a unified framework. Beyond passive monitoring, they analyze context in real time, intercept unsafe actions, dynamically rerouting agent workflows, and enforcing policy compliance across agent interactions. This proactive approach allows enterprises to prevent violations before they escalate.

In this session, we will explore how a control plane for multi-agent AI works in practice, demonstrating scenarios where real-time guardianship enables safe and compliant multi-agent AI at scale.

Hyper-Scale Machine Learning Infrastructure: Training and Inference for Autonomous Vehicles Handling Petabytes of Data per Second

Autonomous vehicles (AVs) continuously generate and process enormous volumes of sensor data, scaling into the petabyte-per-second regime across large fleets. Efficiently managing, training, and deploying machine learning models at such scale presents unprecedented infrastructure challenges.  This presentation explores cutting-edge strategies and technologies for hyper-scale machine learning training and inference, specifically tailored for AV applications. We delve into system architectures, optimized data management techniques, and compute paradigms that enable efficient training, continuous learning, and real-time inference on vast data streams.  Key Topics Covered:  Scalable ML Infrastructure Design: Techniques for parallelization and distributed training across thousands of GPUs and compute nodes.  High-Throughput Data Pipelines: Optimizing data ingestion, preprocessing, labeling, and streaming from AV fleets to centralized data stores.  Resource-Efficient Training: Methods for managing infrastructure resources, minimizing overhead, and maximizing hardware utilization in hyperscale environments.  Real-Time Inference at Scale: Solutions for low-latency inference deployment, edge-to-cloud orchestration, and continuous model updates in large AV fleets.  Case Study – Torc Robotics: Insights from real-world implementations, challenges faced, lessons learned, and future directions based on experiences from Torc Robotics' core ML team.

Propaganda in the Age of Agentic AI: Balancing Innovation and Ethics

Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 have redefined our interaction with technology, showcasing remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding and generation. However, as these models increasingly demonstrate agentic behavior—reasoning, acting, and adapting—they also pose risks, including the potential to generate harmful propaganda, misinformation, and manipulative narratives.

In this talk, Julia will explore the dual-edged nature of agentic AI. Drawing from her recent research, she will highlight real-world examples where LLMs have been misused to spread misleading information and discuss the broader societal implications of these advanced technologies. By examining how AI that reasons, acts, and adapts can be harnessed both constructively and detrimentally, we can better understand the urgent need for robust mitigation strategies.

She will present actionable strategies and innovative approaches aimed at curbing the generation of harmful content, ensuring that these adaptive AI systems are developed and deployed responsibly and ethically. Whether you are an AI practitioner keen on advancing responsible AI practices or someone interested in the societal impacts of adaptive technologies, this session will provide valuable insights into balancing cutting-edge innovation with essential ethical safeguards.

Join her as we delve into how we can collaboratively build safer, more trustworthy agentic AI systems that contribute positively to our digital ecosystem while mitigating the risks of propaganda and misinformation.

jGrK4MVN3fQ.title: Lars Kamp: Monitoring in the Age of GenAI: Beyond Golden Signals
jGrK4MVN3fQ.label: The AI Conference
jGrK4MVN3fQ.description:
The four golden signals (Latency, Errors, Traffic, Saturation) have been the foundation of application monitoring for years, and it still matters, but for GenAI applications, these signals alone leave significant blind spots. A request can return 200 OK with low latency while the response hallucinates, leaks PII, or costs much more than expected. This talk will walk you through what changes when you're monitoring non-deterministic, token-priced, prompt-injectable systems. We'll cover three additional monitoring dimensions — Cost (token attribution, model-mix tracking, wasted spend on failed requests), Safety (prompt injection detection, PII scanning, jailbreak attempts), and Quality (hallucination rate, relevance scoring, user satisfaction) — and show why each one is necessary alongside your existing instrumentation.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

jfCQJVifSYg.title: Kanika Narang, Meta: On-Device LLMs: Power of Conversational AI for Mobile and Wearable Devices

jfCQJVifSYg.description:
Kanika Narang, Research Scientist, Meta

On-Device LLMs: Unleashing the Power of Conversational AI for Mobile and Wearable Devices

Large Language Models (LLMs) have captured the attention of the tech world with their remarkable common-sense reasoning and generalizability. However, their large size and server transfer requirements can make them resource-intensive and slow, which is problematic for use in mobile or wearable devices like smart glasses and smart watches. Moreover, on-device computing could offer a solution to privacy concerns by keeping sensitive data, such as text messages or photos, on the device itself. To tackle these challenges, we’ve developed a more compact language model, ranging from 0.5B to 1.4B parameters. This model is designed to run on-device, providing a competitive performance for conversational grounded tasks, while also managing latency and memory usage effectively. 

In this presentation, I’ll delve into our work on creating a versatile, on-device LLM, which is a distilled version of the LLAMA model, specifically tailored for conversational reasoning tasks. I’ll discuss our pretraining framework and our innovative approach to finetuning, which involves using LLM synthesized, task-specific data in a fresh dialogue format. Finally, I’ll share our strategy for scaling our text-based conversational model to a multimodal model, enhancing generative experiences such as composing text replies, document summarization, image captioning, and visual question-answering on wearables or mobile devices.

kxAetk8gTyw.title: Camila Maia: The Real Cost of Scaling AI: An Inference Playbook
kxAetk8gTyw.label: The AI Conference
kxAetk8gTyw.description:
Training gets the headlines, but inference pays the bills, and for most AI products, it's where margins are won or lost. Today, the vast majority of inference runs on big cloud providers or abstraction platforms, where convenience is high but cost visibility is low. Teams that carefully optimize their models often ship them on infrastructure chosen by default, then discover at scale that their fastest-growing cost is also their least understood. This session is a hands-on framework for understanding inference unit economics in practice. We'll start with the problem every team eventually faces: usage grows, the invoice grows faster, and nobody can quite explain the relationship between the two, because layers of managed abstraction hide the variables that drive cost. The core of the talk is a step-by-step method for making those variables visible. We'll break down how to calculate your true cost per request (not just the sticker price), why utilization — not hardware price — is the number that matters most, and how workload shape (batch vs. real-time, bursty vs. steady, token-heavy vs. compute-light) should drive infrastructure choices. And we'll challenge a common assumption along the way: GPUs aren't the only answer. A growing share of production inference runs efficiently on CPU-only servers, and knowing when that trade-off wins is part of the framework. With the model in hand, we'll map the decision landscape honestly: serverless APIs, managed GPU endpoints, dedicated GPU compute, and CPU-based inference each win in different scenarios, and attendees will get a simple break-even approach for knowing when to move between them. We'll close with a brief look at how these principles play out on dedicated infrastructure: one example of how teams that own their inference stack turn cost from a mystery into a lever. Attendees will walk away with a clear AI infra framework, a checklist for auditing their current inference spend, and a clear-eyed way to answer the question every engineering lead eventually gets asked: "why is our AI bill this high, and what are we doing about it?"

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

With generative AI and large language models (LLM) working alongside healthcare workers of all kinds, we are looking to improve access, equity, and outcomes.

Hippocratic AI is building the industry’s first safety-focused LLM for healthcare, specifically focused on non-diagnostic, patient-facing, real-time healthcare conversation. We present Polaris — an agentic trillion-parameter constellation system with collaborative specialization and safety guardrails for human-like conversation. We will talk about the architecture, specialized training and alignment, and the first comprehensive clinician evaluation of an LLM system for healthcare with thousands of U.S. licensed nurses and hundreds of U.S. licensed physicians. We will also share industry use-cases to showcase the best and safest ways to deploy this technology, and explore what AI- and LLM-powered healthcare could look like in the future.

nsB4SJ73dlg.title: Jaclyn Konzelmann: The Agentic Shift: How to Build Products When AI Can Actually Do Things
nsB4SJ73dlg.label: The AI Conference
nsB4SJ73dlg.description:
We've moved from AI that generates answers to AI that takes actions — and it's broken most of our existing product design playbooks. This talk shares concrete lessons from building agentic AI products at Google Labs, including Project Mariner (an autonomous web agent), Opal (chained AI workflows), and Pomelli (AI marketing for SMBs), alongside a personal experiment: orchestrating a team of 14 AI agents for everything from meal planning to publishing a coloring book on Amazon KDP. The hard-earned lesson? Agentic products live in a year of tensions — exciting vs. overwhelming, autonomy vs. control, thinking big while shipping fast — and the teams that ship well are the ones who design for these tensions instead of pretending they don't exist. What attendees will take away: • A risk framework for agent autonomy based on reversibility, blast radius, and risk type (reputational, monetary, legal) — because "when should the agent ask permission?" is the central design question and the answer is never one-size-fits-all • The "Do It With Me" vs. "Do It For Me" spectrum — a practical model for calibrating how much user involvement any given task should have, with real examples from shipping • Why designing for imperfection matters more than designing for accuracy — agents are non-deterministic systems, and the winning design principle is humans-in-the-loop as a feature, not a fallback • Iterative co-discovery: how users and agents think together, and why scope expansion through collaboration is not scope creep — it is the product working as intended • A proactive design quadrant for finding magic (not Clippy) — when proactive agents feel delightful vs. intrusive, based on task value and user effort This talk is grounded in real product work, real failures, and the honest gap between "AI agent demo" and "AI agent daily driver." No product pitches — just frameworks and lessons from building at both Google scale and personal scale.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

Solving Real Problems for Development Teams with AI

AI coding tools promise productivity gains, but many teams aren’t seeing the impact. The real bottleneck isn’t code generation. It’s context. Understanding why a system was built a certain way, how it evolved, and what trade-offs were made often requires digging through GitHub, Slack, Notion, Confluence, Jira, and other tools. This talk explores the idea of context engineering: structuring and exposing relevant knowledge so both humans and AI agents can work more effectively. I’ll show how Unblocked creates a contextual layer across your tools, giving AI models like Claude and Cursor access to product decisions, architectural history, and team discussions. The result is less hallucination, faster iteration, and fewer interruptions. You get AI that understands your system instead of just guessing. If you’re using AI in production codebases, this is the foundation that makes it work.

Adam Pingel, Head of Open Tools and Applications, AI Alliance

Human/Agent Co-Creation of Shared Knowledge with Semiont

Semiont is a new open-source framework from the AI Alliance that enables humans and intelligent agents to co-create shared knowledge — governed by you and built to last. At its core, Semiont supports the simultaneous co-creation of a wiki and a knowledge graph, allowing text and structured relationships to evolve side by side. On top of this foundation, Semiont provides powerful retrieval and contextualization, drawing on the principles of GraphRAG (Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation).
By weaving together collaborative editing with graph-grounded semantics, Semiont provides a durable framework for meaning-making that goes beyond static documentation or siloed AI memory. Humans and intelligent agents can jointly annotate, connect, and refine entities and relationships, while operators retain full control over what is shared and preserved.
In this talk, I will introduce the core principles behind Semiont, demonstrate its workflows, review its roadmap, and explore the broader implications for sustainable knowledge infrastructure in the age of AI.

Nir Shavit, Professor of Electrical Engineering Computer Science, MIT

The Role of Sparsity in ML

Our brain executes very sparse computation, allowing for great speed and energy savings. Deep neural networks can also be made to exhibit high levels of sparsity without significant accuracy loss. As their size grows, it is becoming imperative that we use sparsity to improve their efficiency. This is a challenging task because the memory systems and SIMD operations that dominate todays CPUs and GPUs do not lend themselves easily to the irregular data patterns sparsity introduces.

This talk will survey the role of sparsity in neural network computation, and the parallel algorithms and hardware features that nevertheless allow us to make effective use of it.

qgGjAw7uDUA.title: Dr. Spencer Torene, Meibel: STAG: Structure Augmented Generation
qgGjAw7uDUA.label: The AI Conference
qgGjAw7uDUA.description:
Dr. Spencer Torene, Principal Research Scientist, Meibel

STAG: Structure Augmented Generation - Bridging Structured and Unstructured Data for Enhanced RAG Systems

Organizations today struggle with extracting insights from diverse data sources, often treating all content as unstructured even when inherent structure exists. We present STAG (STructure Augmented Generation), an innovative system that maximizes performance by automatically identifying and applying structure wherever possible within heterogeneous data collections.   STAG's core philosophy centers on structure-first processing. Rather than treating all content as unstructured by default, STAG identifies structural patterns and relationships that can be leveraged for enhanced retrieval performance. For content that remains genuinely unstructured, STAG creates both graph and table-based representations for discoverable entities in addition to creating traditional RAG embeddings. This dual structural approach applies organizational relationships even to unstructured content, ensuring that retrieval processes benefit from enhanced document context and interconnections.  At query time, STAG's structure-augmented approach delivers superior results by leveraging structured queries where applicable, semantic search where necessary, and automatically incorporating referenced documents through intelligent graph and table traversal. This structural foundation enhances RAG system performance by providing more precise retrieval, better context, and comprehensive responses.  STAG represents a paradigm shift from treating enterprise data as universally unstructured to intelligently applying structure at every opportunity. This approach unlocks significant performance gains in information retrieval and generation by working with data's natural organizational patterns rather than against them. The presentation will demonstrate STAG's architecture, showcase real-world implementation results, and discuss the system's impact on enterprise RAG performance metrics.

sc-11LipM-Q.title: Nathan Wallace: Actions speak louder than prompts: governing what AI agents actually do
sc-11LipM-Q.label: The AI Conference
sc-11LipM-Q.description:
Everyone is watching what goes into AI agents. Almost no one is watching what they actually do. The industry obsesses over the inbound boundary — prompt injection, guardrails, model alignment — while the real risk lands on the other side: the commands an agent runs, the data it moves, the credentials it reaches for, the systems it changes. An agent doesn't need to be jailbroken to cause damage; it just needs to be helpful in the wrong direction. Existing controls can't see this. Every tool in the security stack — secrets managers, DLP, identity, endpoint — watches a boundary: a vault checkout, a network egress, a login. Agents do their work, and their damage, in the space between those boundaries, where every action looks routine and the only identity in sight is a trusted human's. Prompts are too fuzzy to be controls; audit trails are precise but after the fact. Neither answers the question that matters: should this action happen, right now, in this context? This talk makes the case for a new layer: understanding each action an agent is about to take — what will run, what it will touch, and why — and evaluating it before it executes. I'll share real patterns of risky agent behavior from enterprise environments that are invisible to today's tooling. Whether you're enabling AI or governing it, you'll leave with a practical framework for the action layer — and the questions your current stack can't answer.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

uKf0AR-aV6g.title: Robert Chiniquy: Agentic Memory, Logic, and Authorization
uKf0AR-aV6g.label: The AI Conference
uKf0AR-aV6g.description:
This talk introduces a specific, implementable architecture for context-aware agent authorization — using structured memory as a first-class input to the policy evaluation hot path. The core argument is that agent tool calls occupy a gap in the authorization model taxonomy. No single existing model handles them well: RBAC can confirm a user has a role that includes Jira access, but cannot scope a tool call to a specific project without creating a role per project. ABAC can evaluate request parameters against static constraints, but requires someone to have pre-configured those constraints — it doesn't know why project ALPHA is the right scope. ReBAC can traverse a relationship graph to determine that a user is related to project ALPHA through a team, but doesn't account for temporal context (the user was on ALPHA last quarter, now on BETA). The missing input is situational context: what is this user currently working on? What has their agent been doing in this session? What tools do people in this user's role typically use? The talk will present: A memory architecture designed for authorization — not general-purpose agent memory. Three typed stores (worker memory from identity/HR/project systems, agent session memory from conversation context, organizational baseline memory from usage analytics), each with different trust levels, update semantics, and confidence scoring. Temporal validity ranges on every fact for point-in-time audit queries. This draws on and synthesizes ideas from the academic agent memory literature (Zep/Graphiti for temporal knowledge graphs, Hindsight for belief evolution with confidence, MIRIX for typed multi-agent stores) but is purpose-built for the authorization use case. A write/read split architecture for the hot path. Memory facts are extracted asynchronously (tolerating LLM latency for fact extraction and confidence scoring). Authorization decisions are evaluated synchronously against pre-compiled facts using Datalog — deterministic, terminating, auditable, sub-millisecond. The evaluation does not call an LLM. It does not make network round-trips to external stores. The facts are local and pre-compiled. Memory-informed delegation policies. Concrete Datalog examples showing how a delegation can reference memory predicates instead of static parameter constraints. A rule that says "allow this Jira create_issue call if the target project is one the user is currently working on, per memory, with confidence above 0.7" — and if confidence is below the threshold, escalate to a human approval flow. Plus anomaly detection via organizational memory baselines: "this tool is not typical for this user's role" as a governance signal, not a hard deny. An honest treatment of the unsolved problems — particularly the local authentication and configuration barrier for non-technical users, and the challenge of governing memory itself (provenance, retention, review cycles) when memory facts influence authorization decisions.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

About Peter Norvig
Peter Norvig is a Distinguished Education Fellow at Stanford's Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute and a researcher at Google Inc; previously he directed Google's core search algorithms group and Google's Research group. He was head of NASA Ames's Computational Sciences Division, where he was NASA's senior computer scientist and a recipient of NASA's Exceptional Achievement Award in 2001. He has taught at the University of Southern California, Stanford University, and the University of California at Berkeley, from which he received a Ph.D. in 1986 and the distinguished alumni award in 2006. He was co-teacher of an Artificial Intelligence class that signed up 160,000 students, helping to kick off the current round of massive open online classes. His publications include the books Data Science in Context (to appear in 2022), Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (the leading textbook in the field), Paradigms of AI Programming: Case Studies in Common Lisp, Verbmobil: A Translation System for Face-to-Face Dialog, and Intelligent Help Systems for UNIX. He is also the author of the Gettysburg Powerpoint Presentation and the world's longest palindromic sentence. yLGKaFZ69vE.title: Manqing Liu: Post-Training LLMs for Entertainment: Engagement, Safety & Non-Verifiable Rewards
yLGKaFZ69vE.label: The AI Conference
yLGKaFZ69vE.description:
Training LLMs for entertainment applications, such as AI characters and interactive storytelling, presents a unique opportunity: how to develop models that are engaging and safe. Measuring model responses is a specialization where there is not merely a set universe of objective criteria, as in other fields. As a result, we often use signals from user behavior, such as swipe interactions and whether a user continues the conversation or disengages, to infer preferences and guide model improvements. This talk will explore how we approach post-training in this setting using reinforcement learning with real-world user interaction data. We will discuss how to identify which user behaviors are meaningful and how to use them to improve models despite the lack of a clear ground truth. We will share practical techniques for balancing multiple goals. This includes methods for structuring training so the model learns from both positive signals (e.g., continued engagement) and negative signals (e.g., undesirable outputs), as well as strategies for prioritizing different objectives at different stages of training. We will also cover how testing and training models on difficult prompts helps uncover weaknesses and improve reliability in real-world use, and how improvements discovered in larger models can be transferred to smaller, more efficient models without sacrificing performance. Grounded in real-world implementation, this session will provide a clear framework for training and improving LLMs in domains where success is difficult to measure directly. Attendees will leave with practical approaches to working with imperfect user feedback, balancing competing objectives, and applying these methods to production AI systems.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved
